why-local-ocr-is-the-future.content:
You photograph a marksheet. A site says "upload for OCR." That file is now on someone else's disk. Maybe they delete it. Maybe they don't.

That's the whole argument for reading text in the browser.

### Why cloud OCR feels convenient — and isn't
The server has a fat model. You wait. You get text. You also gave them a bank statement, or an Aadhaar page, or a doctor's scan. For a public flyer, fine. For ID, I'd rather the pixels never leave this laptop.

### What actually runs here
[PDF OCR](/tools/pdf-ocr/) uses a model in the tab (Tesseract in WebAssembly). The page is drawn, letters are guessed, you copy the text. Close the tab and the file is gone from memory — we never received a copy.

It's slower on a 80-page scan than a datacenter. That's the trade.

### When to use it
Receipts, form scans, a page you need to paste into Excel. Don't expect magic on a crumpled photocopy. If the scan is sideways, rotate it first.

pipeline.title: On-Device Sandbox Pipeline
pipeline.subtitle: Click through each stage to see how files are isolated and processed entirely inside your active tab context.
pipeline.step1_desc: You select your files. The browser loads them into local memory (RAM) directly inside the tab. No network packets are sent to the internet.
pipeline.step2_desc: Heavy compilation engines (written in C++ or Rust) load directly as WebAssembly (WASM) modules. They execute locally on your processor.
pipeline.step3_desc: The processing runs inside the browser's isolated tab thread, completely separated from other tabs and your operating system's files.
pipeline.step4_desc: The output file is written directly from RAM back to your device. The connection is instant and requires zero server queues.
